utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have appearances, starting with the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, counsel. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. Mark Harmon, Bronagh McKenna and Carmela Javier appearing for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. Representing Mr. Perisic's Defence today is represented by Tina Drolec, Milos Androvic, Daniela Tasic, Gregor Guy-Smith, and Novak Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Before I call the witness, Your Honour, I have a request of the Court and that is I would request that the witness be permitted to have the text of the Law on the Army and the Law on Defence in front of him. He is going to be referring to it frequently and rather than have him to look at a screen and a monitor and go back and forth between the document it would be easier and more convenient for him if these could be in his presence in front of him. I have shown these to the Defence. The Defence has no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you confirm, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would kindly ask for a copy, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Interpreters are kindly asking for a copy but the interpreters did not interpret what Mr. Lukic told us.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what Mr. Lukic, Ms. Interpreter?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Perhaps Mr. Lukic can repeat what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you repeat yourself, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Harmon showed me the documents and we don't have any objection for the witness to have the hard copy of the document in front him.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreters apologise once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. -- they are forgiven. Thank you. Then you can let the witness have the documents there. Thank you, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we will process now of arranging copies for the booth, so if I could have just one minute, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- then we'll call the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How is the Chamber going to view those documents? Are they going to be on the screen or are we going to receive hard copies too?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. What I intend to do is, he will refer to particular articles in the documents that will be called up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I now can call the next witness, Miodrag Starcevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. Would Your Honours prefer to have hard copies of these laws?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No. As -- we in your hands, Mr. Harmon --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- we don't know what --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May you please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I may have the assistance of the usher to give Mr. Starcevic copies of both the Law on Defence and the Law on the Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, the usher will be handing copies in your language of the Law on Defence and the Law on the Army and feel free during course of your examination to refer to particular articles when you feel it necessary or when I direct you to do so. Now, Mr. Starcevic, could you, first of all, state your full name and spell your last name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: My last name is Starcevic, S-t-a-r-c-e-v-i-c or C. My name is Miodrag.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: The 29th of April, 1945.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And your nationality?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you describe for us your educational background.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I completed high school and the military technical academy. After completion of the military technical academy, I graduated at the faculty of law. I studied in Zagreb and Split. I have a masters from the faculty of law in Belgrade, and I have a Ph.D. also from the faculty of law in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you just tell us the years when you received those various degrees in law.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, I graduated at the faculty of law in 1978. 1978. I think that I completed my masters in 1987 or 1988 -- I'm sorry, excuse me. And I completed my Ph.D. in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Starcevic, I would like to focus on your military career. First of all, how many years did you serve in the military?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I joined the Military Academy in 1964. I completed it in 1967. I left the army formally in March 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So is it a correct statement to say that you served both in the JNA and in the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you please review your military career, identifying the significant posts and the duties and responsibilities associated with each of those posts.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of my military career, I worked as an officer in the technical service. This means that from 1967 onwards, until the day I graduated at the faculty of law in 1978, or 1977, I worked there on regular duties in that service, meaning that I was a commander of the platoon for technical maintenance. I was a desk officer of the technical service in the relevant units, and I was the chief of the technical service in similar unit. After graduating, I got involved in legal tasks, in military institutions in the Split garrison, which was, in essence, a military construction institution. I was in charge of the general and the personnel service there. I'm not sure, but I think in 1980 or 1981, I transferred from Split to the Belgrade garrison, and I worked in the personnel administration of the then Federal Secretariat for National Defence, and I was assigned to tasks in the second degree appeals process, where I was preparing the proceedings in the appeals of officers to individual personnel decisions or appointments. After a few years, I think two or three years later, I moved to the legal administration of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, where I worked for a few years as a secretary of the higher military disciplinary court, and I worked on legislative assignments and international law and international relations. I cannot remember the exact date, but some time in the early 1990s, I became the deputy of the chief -- I became chief deputy of the personnel administration, and I continued to work on similar assignments, with the exception of the military disciplinary court. I think that as the Deputy Chief I was also the editor-in-chief of the military gazette, but I'm not sure if I was performing that job as the Deputy Chief or later as the chief. In 1992, after the then chief retired, I became the chief of that administration, the legislative administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is in the legal department; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What were your duties in that particular capacity?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I was the secretary of the military disciplinary court where I conducted, organised, prepared materials and provided advice to members of the court on legal matters. As far as the legislative tasks were concerned, I was working on the then Law on the Service in the Military Armed Forces and also the then Law on National People's Defence which meant that I had to monitor the implementation of that law, assist the senior officers in the units and in institutions and in the Federal Secretariat and others who referred to me for requests for opinion pertaining to certain problems in the application of those laws. And, of course, I monitored possible problems that would crop up in the application of the laws, and simply to maintain records on the frequency of such problems, and possibly to initiate changes and amendments to the laws. Of course, I was also in charge of administrative and professional tasks, when the laws were amended or changed. At the same time during debates on the laws in the then assembly, I was available to answer questions that were being asked in relation to certain solutions. As for the work related to international law and international relations, it was my duty to monitor international contracts, primarily in the field of international humanitarian law, and to propose measures for the implementation of that law in the armed forces of the then Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you assist drafting legislation in respect of international humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, it was my task in the administrative sense to manage those assignments, to consult people who were able to help, and in a way to direct all of those activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, did you remain the chief of this particular section until your retirement?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the formal legal sense, yes. I remained at that position, but I think early in 1994, or in late 1993, I submitted my request to retire from service, and practically on the same day, when I submitted this request to the Defence minister, I informed the members of the department about it, and I asked my deputy to take over, even though in the formal legal sense I continued to be the chief of the legal department but I did not actually perform any duties there any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, if I can turn now to your post-military career. Can you explain to the Court what your jobs have been or your responsibilities and functions and tasks have been that has occupied your career since you left the military?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: For a few months, I didn't have any work, and I must admit, I didn't really try that hard to look for work. As it happened, I was volunteered [as interpreted] in the Red Cross of Yugoslavia, even from the time when I arrived in Belgrade, even when I was professionally still a military man, I assisted the Red Cross, primarily on some legal matters. I was a member of the Red Cross commission for international humanitarian law. And some time in late May or early June 1994, I was asked to join the Red Cross, because the previous legal advisor of the Yugoslav Red Cross had retired. I didn't hesitate to accept this job, and as of June 1994, practically until 2005, I believe - yes, 2005 - I worked as a professional in the Yugoslav Red Cross. Parallel with that and after I left the army, I continued my teaching duties at the Military Academy. I was a lecturer at the Military Academy in a subject called military law and regulations, which encompassed teaching the Military Academy students about these laws and other regulations that are applied in the army, as well as teaching on international humanitarian. At the same time, when I was working in the Red Cross, I was working as a professor, a guest professor or lecturer, at some universities when they required me to give lectures from international humanitarian law. For example, the faculty of political sciences in Belgrade, a post-graduate studies programme there. I participated also in commissions for the Ph.D. and masters thesis examinations at the Military Academy. I also gave lectures abroad, mostly at seminars and gatherings organised by the International Red Cross. For example, I went to the Warsaw School of Humanitarian Law, and I went also to some other places. I was quite active as a member of the International Institute for Humanitarian Law in San Remo and I took part in many gatherings and meetings at that institute. That's more or less it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you occupy your time in any writing of books, treatises?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I wrote books just like all people who are in that field. I published a few books. Also scores of professional and expert papers, and I gave presentations at international meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you a member of any professional associations?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm a member of the Association for International Law in Belgrade. Earlier the association was called the Yugoslav Association for International Law. I'm a member of the International Law Association in London, and I'm a member of the International Institute for Humanitarian Law in San Remo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, thank you for that comprehensive discussion about your background. What I'd like to do now is focus your attention on the defence structures in both the SFRY and the FRY, and what I'd like to do is ask you to describe, if you will, the defence structure in the SFRY. In the course of doing so, could you kindly describe the relationship between the federal government, the Presidency, the Federal Secretariat of National Defence, and the General Staff of the army. Just tell us how it worked.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I must say that the question is not a simple and easy one but I will try to remember -- to respond according to my best recollection. I assume that the question refers to the time-period before the then new constitution went into effect, meaning it was 1992, when the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was still in existence. So in the former SFRY, formally, the Federal Secretariat for National Defence was a part of the Federal Executive Council, and it was an organ of executive power. So, in those relations, the Federal Secretariat of National Defence was, in a way, subordinate to the then president of the Federal Executive Council, or rather, the prime minister. And from a formal legal aspect, it was part of, conditionally speaking, the civilian authorities, the civilian structure. On the other side, there was some unclarified aspect of this order because at the time the General Staff of the then Yugoslavia was an organisational part of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence. At the same time, the highest command organ in the armed forces of the then SFRY was the Presidency of the SFRY, which, at the time, comprised six or eight members. I think it was eight members. I think the autonomous provinces had their own representatives. There were six republics and two autonomous provinces. In any case, it was the Presidency as a collective organ. Along that line of command, it was authorised to command. So legally, the situation was not quite clear, as far as these relationships were concerned. Practically, or actually, the chief of the General Staff was, in a way, subordinated to the Federal Secretariat for National Defence. Of course, the chief of the General Staff in the system also had the authority to command over all the units and institutions in the then Army of Yugoslavia. In order for the situation to be even more complicated, there was also the territorial component of the armed forces or, rather, the republics had units of the so-called Territorial Defence. They had their Territorial Defence at whose head were the Republican Staffs for Territorial Defence. Although, if I remember correctly, pursuant to the Law on General People's Defence, the republics did not have any special authority, as far as command over that territorial component was -- over the Territorial Defence, rather, but that line of command formally was a single line of command going from the Presidency down. In practice, there was also a tendency for the republican administrations or the republican authorities to have a quite significant influence over the work of those staffs and units and institutions and particularly through certain rights in the logistics and supply of those units and the influence on personnel affairs, and so on and so forth. This means that there was quite a lot of overlapping and lack of clarity, as far as establishing clear legal relationships, and this was particularly pronounced before the beginning of the armed conflicts in the then SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was there an effort or a decision taken to clarify this confusing structure and this confusing set of relationships?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know that such efforts were made. However, I was not involved in those activities because these related primarily to the problems in the command and control structure, but as part and a member of the legal administration, and as a person who was in charge of, among other things, the Law on Defence, I could observe from time to time that certain steps were being taken that were aimed at resolving these unresolved issues. Primarily, in the command and control structure, and the relationship between the federal level and the level of the republics, but sometimes also within those particular units. There was a well-known situation where a commander of the staff of Territorial Defence of a republic would be on a collision course with the republic authorities, where he was trying to perform his duties as a professional soldier but then he was unable to do so because of the republican authorities's involvement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, did -- Mr. Starcevic, did the structure change at a certain point in time and were new relationships created and defined?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The structure changed substantially when the new constitution was adopted. When I say "new," I mean the new constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia which explicitly set forth that the chain of command ran from the president, down to the military organs, the Chief of Staff, and then to the lower level -- lowest level units. In keeping with that, and before the laws that I have in front of me were adopted, the Presidency took a strategic decision on reorganising the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. When did this new constitutions come into place? Can you give us dates for this, when the new constitution came in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I cannot give you the exact date but as far as I can recall, I believe this was in April 1992. I think I'm right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You were saying, Mr. Starcevic, that the Presidency took a strategic decision on reorganising the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It took the decision on reorganisation that was to put in place the provisions of the constitution. The basic purpose of that decision was to clearly define the competencies and separate the competencies between the federal Ministry of Defence under the new constitution and the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army. Generally speaking, this -- this line of separation was to proceed from the fact that the federal ministry was part of the federal government, and that, as part of that federal government, it was in fact part of the mechanism that establishes and implements policies in the area of defence. In other words, the Ministry of Defence in this new organisation was supposed to, together -- as well as the federal government, to adopt decisions and provide guidelines in the sphere of defence, to provide the legal basis for it, provide logistics and everything else that is required, in the same way that the federal government functioned in other areas. On the other hand, the General Staff was supposed to be an operational organ in charge of operational tasks of the army; in other words, the essential military work, the preparation of units and their employment, and so on, and to make sure that there is no overlapping of competencies in this field. Under this new concept, the Ministry of Defence would not have any authority in commanding the army; whereas the General Staff would have had no influence on the political aspects of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So the new structures that were created made a clear distinction between the command relationship in the army, and from what I understand your testimony to be, the Ministry of Defence no longer had any command authority over the army. It was more to deal with issues of logistics, personnel, et cetera. Is that a fair and correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part. However, no new bodies were established. Rather, the already existing bodies were assigned certain competencies or authorities in this manner, and I wouldn't want to omit mentioning here that the Ministry of Defence still maintained as one of its primary functions the legislative aspects of defence. In other words, the preparation of and drafting of proposals to the federal government of regulations and bills that were supposed to be passed. However, this, too, should not be understood to mean that the General Staff was to be completely excluded from these job, from this work. On the contrary, the General Staff was supposed to participate in and was supposed to give their own proposals in the course of preparation of certain new regulations, but the ministry was the final decision-maker on whether these proposals would be adopted or not, and the content of these new regulations. The bills, the regulations that were in the bills, that would of course then be forwarded to the government because the government was the final instance that proposed all these bills to the parliament that is then to adopt them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now you have in front of you two laws, the Law on the Army, and the Law on Defence. And let me ask you: What was the relationship between the change in the constitution, in the new constitution, and the promulgation of these laws?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: In effect, these laws provided a legal basis for a decision that had already been made by the Presidency, and they were providing a legal framework for the bill of the Presidency on reorganisation. In this -- at this point in time, in the form of a new law.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I want to take each of these documents separately. First of all, focussing on just the Law on the Army. Mr. Starcevic, are you familiar, first of all, with those laws, and -- first of all, are you familiar with the laws and the contents of the law?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, generally speaking, I am. I have forgotten many parts, but I hope I can refresh my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what role, if any, did you have in the creation, in the drafting of the Law on the Army?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I have already mentioned, it was my job, in fact, to do that, and I was a member of the team. In this particular case, I was the leader of the team, the team of the legal department, legal administration that was involved in drafting this law. Of course, the legal administration was not the only body that was involved in drafting this law. Our job, our team's job and our administration's job was to actually provide the final bill, and this proposed law has certain areas where lawyers, in fact, cannot be experts in every particular area. In such instances, we would ask for experts to provide their initial proposals, and then we tried to incorporate those proposals provided by experts and incorporate them in the legal solutions. In other words, we were not to propose anything that was in conflict with the constitution and with some general legal framework, and in some jobs, some tasks, which were of a purely legal nature, we were the main body that formulated certain regulations or certain provisions that dealt with those issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Turning your attention to the Law on Defence, I have the same question: What role did you play in the drafting and -- of that particular legislation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: More or less it was the same role as in the case with the Law on the Army, and of course, I would like to stress one more time that we were not experts in, for instance, the organisation of units, the military tasks and operational duties, and in such tasks, we also sought expert opinion and expert proposals, in this instance this would have been mainly from the General Staff, and from our military schools and other military experts. But, again, we made sure that solutions that were in conflict with the constitution were not put forth as a proposal, which were in conflict with the constitution or other general laws. So, in other words, as an administration after reviewing all the proposals and the possible solutions we would draft the final bill, forward it to the federal government to review, accept and perhaps amend, and then they would forward it to the parliament for adoption.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When did the Law on the Army become effective, what date?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: There is an problem here that I need to explain. The parliament of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at the time was a two-chamber parliament. It had two chambers. One of those was the Chamber of Nations and the other was the Chamber of Republics. A bill could only be adopted if it was adopted in its identical form at both chambers. During parliamentary debates it so happened that the Chamber of Citizens - I apologise, not the Chamber of Nations but Chamber of Citizens - adopted the bill on the Law on Defence; whereas the Chamber of republics, I believe, which was held on the next day, in any case after the other chamber, amended some provision of this bill. I can't recall at this point in time what the amendment was, but the fact remains that this law was not adopted in its identical form at both chambers. In such events, the constitution envisaged that the text adopted at the citizens' chamber would be in effect, but on condition that within a year those two texts would have to be collated. So, in other words, this law came into effect in the form that it was adopted in at the Chamber of Citizens at the end of May, I believe, 19 -- no, I apologise, in October 1993. And the final adjustments -- the final amendments and the final adjustments were made in May 1994, so that in fact there are two dates when this law came into effect, in practice. The first text that was adopted in October 1993; and then the amended and the coordinated text that was adopted in May 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So if I understand, Mr. Starcevic, the coordinated text that was adopted in May of 1994 essentially reconciled the one article where there had been different language?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And in all other particulars, the Law on the Army became effective in October of 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you've testified a bit about how the law -- how these laws altered the defence structure. What I'd like to do is turn to Prosecution Exhibit P1183.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If that could be --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's the Law on Defence, Mr. Starcevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 4 of the B/C/S on that, and on page -- starting on page 5 of the -- of the English version. If we could -- yes. No, I think -- I want to focus on in English text, starting at chapter 5 on the lower right-hand corner, president of the republic. And then focus on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Does this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, chapter 5 or chapter 4?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Chapter 4, I'm sorry. This is very small text. Chapter 4, Your Honour, please, and then after Your Honours have had an opportunity to review that, if we could then turn to the next page, because I want to refer Your Honours to Articles 42 and 43 and 44.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, while the Court is looking at that and -- let me just ask you, referring to Articles 40, 41, 42, and 43 on the Law on Defence, does this text define the rights and the duties of the various state organs; in other words, the president of the republic, the Supreme Defence Council, the federal government, and the federal Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These articles provide for precisely that, and that is what they define.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And so when you were talking about the separation of the organs, one would find the parameters of the -- of the duties and responsibilities and functions of those organs in these -- in the texts of these particular articles; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in conjunction with this text, if we could turn to another exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It's Prosecution Exhibit 197, which is the Law on the Army, and I'm specifically interested in page 13 of the B/C/S and page 37 of the English. No, I think that's not correct. What I'm interested in -- I'm interested in article -- this is the Law on the Army. I'm interested in Articles 4, 5, and 6, so I assume it's at the front of the text. I'm sorry, I don't have the exact page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, if you can occupy yourself with the text on Articles 4, 5, and 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could turn, first of all, to Article 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Does this article define who commanded the army in times of war and peace and what the tasks and responsibilities were of the president of the republic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I refrained from reacting so far, but I hope Mr. Harmon will not get into the practice of asking this type of questions. He could ask the witness what this article was about, but we've seen that on several occasions until now, Mr. Harmon has sort of summed up the question for the witness and then just asked him to confirm. In other words, I am afraid that we are going into situation where Mr. Harmon is analysing these -- these things, and just asking the witness to confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no problem with that, Your Honour. I will rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, I want to focus on Article 4. Can you explain Article 4 to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Article 4 defines the competencies of the president of the republic in commanding. In other words, it defines that the president of the republic shall command the army and it also mentions all the tasks that the president does, in order to command the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could -- if I could direct your attention to Article 5, could you explain to the Court the Article 5 and what it established in the new order of -- and the new structures?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: In Article 5, the law defines the role and position of the General Staff of the army and describes it as the highest and professional staff organ for the preparation and use of the army in times of peace and war. And, of course, again, in the same manner as we have seen in Article 4, it defines the types of tasks that the chief of the General Staff has to perform in order to -- to carry out the role as defined by the Law of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, if I can direct your attention finally to Article 6, can you explain Article 6 and its relationship to the new structures and new order?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: In essence, Article 6 provides the authority of the chief of the General Staff to pass -- to issue certain rules which would actually be the implementation of certain enactments by the president of the republic, providing for the command of the army. In fact, this article also defines the role of other officers and their duties in commanding their own units and institutions, in keeping with this law and the enactments that were passed by their superior officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, under this statutory scheme, what was the relationship then of the VJ General Staff to the other organs?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not certain -- I'm not sure that I understood your question in this particular case. If you're referring to other General Staff bodies, that relationship is quite clear. However, if you were referring to bodies that were outside the General Staff, then that is not provided for in these articles. If you were referring to relationships with units and institutions of the army, the chief of the General Staff has a general authority to command all units of the army, pursuant to decisions adopted by the president of the republic. However, if you were referring to other bodies then --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, let me clarify the question and what I intended to ask. In relation to the president of the republic and the Supreme Defence Council, where did the General Staff, the chief of the General Staff fit in the line of subordination?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: The chief of the General Staff is subordinated to the president of the republic, who is the one who executes the command. In a way, he is also subordinated to the Supreme Defence Council, in view of the fact that the president of the republic commands the army pursuant to decisions of the Defence Council. However, if I may be permitted to state my own opinion, it seems to me that the direct relationship is established only between the president of the republic and the chief of the General Staff in view of the principles of command in the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to refer -- in the same Law on the Army, I'd like to refer you, Mr. Starcevic, to Article 151.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Article 151 is found on page 13 of the B/C/S and page 37 of the English. You can see it is, unfortunately, just at the bottom so we're going -- in the English version. The text goes over to the next page, so, Your Honours -- when Your Honours have finished reading that text, if we could go to the next page and enlarge the top portion of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Starcevic, if I could kindly ask you to explain to the Court what Article 151 is and what it is -- its purpose is?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Article 151 regulates the authority of the president of the republic in implementing the tasks, which, in our legal system, the legislature in Serbia and the former Yugoslavia are called administrative jobs, jobs that imply making decisions on the rights and duties of professional officers, professional soldiers, rather. Those are the assignments relating to decisions on promotions of personnels, appointments to certain positions and duties, transfers, and it's important to note that these are tasks that are formally established, are carried out according to a legal procedure that is previously established, and that provide for at least two stages of decision-making. So there has to be a two-step decision, and in most cases, there is the right to appeal and the right to legal protections.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We will cover -- I'm going to cover that particular subject matter area that you have mentioned, the right to legal protections and the right to appeal, later in my examination, Mr. Starcevic. Now, let me direct your attention now to Article 152. Could you kindly explain to the Trial Chamber the purpose and the intent of Article 152 and how it relates to the new structure and new order?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Article 52 [as interpreted] also deals with the authorities for the execution of those same tasks. Except in this case, in order to perform those tasks, the person in charge is the chief of the General Staff. However, not only the chief of the General Staff, but also the senior officers at units in institutions that he authorises for that purpose, meaning that the chief of the General Staff probably directly carries out some of these tasks and authorises his subordinate officers of units and institutions to carry out other tasks. It is important to note that dealing with these matters in the Army of Yugoslavia was always something that depended on ranks or the position that those persons occupy. So different officers would be authorised to decide on the promotion of non-commissioned officers, and, in principle, that would be a matter of lower rank; while the promotions of, let's say, colonels or higher officers, would be decided by some more senior-ranking officers, perhaps who were in the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Starcevic, this statutory scheme and these relationships, the new defined relationships where the Ministry of Defence is separated from the command responsibilities that you have testified about, did that structure remain in place or did that eventually change? Or are these laws that you have described identifying and defining the relationships and the functions of the president, the Supreme Defence Council, the chief of the General Staff, did that system -- does that system remain today?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: If you're thinking of this system that was established pursuant to this law, I hope that it has been retained, but I cannot assert that, because I actually left the army in the interim period when one of the laws expired and the other went into effect, so I'm not really that familiar right now with how things function in the army. I am hoping that it is so, though, because this is something that is provided under the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we can now -- I'm going to turn to a different subject, Your Honour, and I'll start my examination but we will -- if we could break at 10.15, then I can cover five minutes of the new subject right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, I want to turn to the subject of personnel centres right now, and what I'd like to do is, first of all, refer to these laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Again, I'd like to go back to Article 5 of the Law on the Army. And if we could go back ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you aware, Mr. Starcevic, that two special personnel centres were created, the 30th Personnel Centre and the 40th Personnel Centre?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I know that now but at the time that I was still in active service, I didn't know that until almost the end of the service, even if then, perhaps it was only after I completed by service, but I wasn't really aware of it. And it was not my duty or obligation or right to know something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you comment, or are you able to give us any insight as to why you didn't know about the creation of the 30th and 40th Personnel Centres?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Simply because I was serving in the Ministry of Defence, and the chief of the General Staff, according to Article 5, has the authority to establish the organisation of the army and the units and institutions of the army, so that is under the authority of the General Staff, and by the nature of things, I did not have to be informed. And perhaps I wasn't even supposed to be informed because that is the authority that is in the ambit of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you, Mr. Starcevic, if you could point to the -- inform the Court what the legal basis is for the creation of new units within the VJ. Can you point -- direct the Court to the particular statutory authority?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Article 5, item 2, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Of which law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of the Law on the Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me -- Mr. Perisic [sic], you indicate that the authority is in Article 5, item 2, paragraph 2, and I have an English translation that indicates that item 2 is -- states: "Determine the plan of recruitment and maintenance of manpower levels for the army and the numerical distribution of recruits in the army." So there may have been a translation error or there may have been -- is that what you intended to refer to is that text I read or is there a different text?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I actually had the opportunity to see there was a mistake in the interpretation. I said Article 5, paragraph 2, item 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, then I -- let me read you --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Again, the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can I read a text to you if -- actually, can you read the text, Mr. Starcevic, that establishes the authority of the General Staff of the -- chief of the General Staff to establish new units, can you read the text that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'd just like to note that the mistake in the transcript was repeated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To help, there is really the interpreter's mistake here. It is a legal terminology perhaps in that sense we can clarify and we can help. When the witness said item 2 -- or paragraph 2, item 3 [as interpreted], in our interpretation of the regulation, when he says paragraph 2, it means paragraph 2, which does not have a numerical marking; but when he said item, he meant the paragraph that is numerically marked and he said item 1. So in that way, paragraph is a part of the article which is not marked by a number, and the item is the part of the article that does have a numerical marking.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Starcevic, just so can completely eliminate any possibility of confusion, can you read the text in Article 5 that gives the chief of the General Staff the authority to establish units in the army?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to try to read the paragraph without which you cannot understand the item. So the chief of the General Staff, in accordance with the basic principles of the organisation, development and establishment of the army and the documents issued by the president of the republic shall, (1), determine the organisation, plan of development, and establishment of the commands, units, and institutions of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Starcevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this would be a convenient time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is, indeed. We will take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If Prosecution Exhibit P733 could be placed on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, this is a document I want to show you, first of all, give you an opportunity to look at the front page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And then if we could go to the second page to the signature line, and then return to the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 15th of November, 1993, on organisational and formational changes in the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if we could turn to the second -- the signature page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This document, sir, has a signature line under chief of the VJ General Staff, Colonel General Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now could we return to the first page of each document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, can you, first of all, examine this document. Have you examined this document? Have you had a chance to look at the document, sir? This is -- first of all, sir, this -- is this document an order?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's -- well, again, we have the problem of understanding the difference between an order, as a document, and an order, as a document. There is a difference in B/C/S between "naredba" and "naredjenje." This implies that it's a general act, "naredba," which does not decide on the duties and obligations, but it's a document on the establishment of a new unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So this is a -- is this document consistent with the authorities and competencies of General Perisic under Article 5 that we looked at just before the break?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And as you can see in this document, Mr. Starcevic, there is two new formations established, a 30th Personnel Centre and a 40th Personnel Centre. Can you -- do you see that in the text under item 1 and item 2?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where was the peacetime location of each of those Personnel Centres, according to this document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: According to the document, the Belgrade garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was there a designation for the 30th Personnel Centre in times of peace, a numerical designation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. From what I can understand, that is the designation cited in the order, military post 3001.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we scroll down in the B/C/S. Actually, we need to go to the next page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is there a numerical designation for the 40th Personnel Centre in this particular document?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, could you comment on subpart --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Actually, we need to go to the second page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, sir, we had earlier looked at some legal texts. Could you comment on subpart 3 of the text before you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Paragraph 3 indicates that the chief of the General Staff certifies certain tasks, deployment and other issues essential for the work and -- of the Personnel Centres in collaboration with the General Staff organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Does -- earlier we looked at a text, a legal text that said that the chief of the General Staff could delegate certain functions and duties to other elements under his command. Do you recall that text?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is item number 3 an example of such a delegation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I think that generally you can say yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic complained just before the break that you formulate your questions to elicit a response rather than suggest a question --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will be more careful, Your Honour. Thank you. I'd like to take a look at another document. It is Prosecution Exhibit 524. That's not the -- no, that's -- I'm sorry. It is Prosecution Exhibit 734.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Starcevic, have you seen this document before coming into court?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was shown to me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And could we go to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, let me, first of all, ask you, do you recall this document, Mr. Starcevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Generally yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. And under the general work principles of special Personnel Centres, I'd like to direct your attention to item number 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we turn to item number 7 and show that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Starcevic, can you comment on subpart 7 for us?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Subpart 7, in my opinion, means that these instructions regulate the work of the Personnel Centres in peacetime and do not refer to regulating the work in combat or conditions of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hear the interpretation referring to peacetime. Do we see peace time anywhere in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, can you answer Judge Moloto's question?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not directly mentioned, no, but from the text one can make that conclusion. The text literally states that these instructions shall not regulate the wartime organisation and establishment of the army, command and control, and execution of immediate missions in the combat operations of individual units, meaning that what happens outside of peacetime activities is something that these instructions do not regulate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And there is reference in this particular text and throughout this document to Personnel Centre Main Staffs. You see the reference, for example, in subpart 7. Can you interpret the meaning of "Personnel Centre Main Staffs"?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid that I'm not fully competent to do that. My military expertise, which is not large, says that units of the Army of Yugoslavia do have staffs and chiefs of those staffs; but in this particular case, I don't know what this would refer to because I cannot see it from this very document, and that is why it would be necessary to see the whole organisational structure and establishment. Simply, according to what I know, this is just a matter of language. But whether it actually relates to some other matters, I really cannot judge that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is it common, Mr. Starcevic, in other formations within the VJ, particular units, to have Main Staffs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that Mr. Harmon is now trying to lead the witness, because he is not satisfied with the answer that the witness gave, and I think he should re-word his question and be more precise, because this looks very leading to me. I don't wish to comment any further because I don't want to lead. But I think that this is a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I don't think it is a leading question, Your Honour. Mr. Starcevic spent many years in the service. He's familiar with the army. The question wasn't leading. It was an inquiry as to whether or not certain structures existed in units in the army with which he is very familiar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The objection is overruled.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to say that, as far as I can recall, I did not run across this language in practice, the term "General Staff." I did come across the term, perhaps, "staff," if that is the answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me -- can I be -- can I be concrete --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The witness said Main Staff, not General Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. That answers the question then. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, then examining both the last two documents that we have looked at, both the instructions and the -- the order relating to organisational and formational changes in the VJ, are those documents, on their face, lawful?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to make an objection to this question. I really feel that this type of question is not in accordance with your decision of yesterday, Your Honour. I understood your decision to mean that the witness can be asked for his personal opinions, and Mr. Harmon did ask the question -- did ask this witness questions about his experiences and things that he saw and knew of, which can be a basis for the witness's conclusions. But I think that with this question, Mr. Harmon is actually asking the witness to ask a question that is without -- that is outside the framework of what a fact witness can testify to. The witness himself said that he didn't know anything about the Personnel Centres, nor did he have any factual knowledge of them, so now what he is being asked to do is to draw conclusions based on something that is not -- that does not arise from his own personal experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: May I re-frame the question, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In fact, I think this question has been answered already. You asked the witness now after the break if these instructions were according to Article 5 of the law, and he said yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's fine. I mean, that -- as to one particular aspect of it. I'm satisfied to withdraw the question. I don't think there would be a difficulty. But, nevertheless, I will withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, let me now ask you, were -- according to these documents, persons who were assigned to these Personnel Centres, were they members of the VJ, according to law?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, what I'd like to do is go into private session, Your Honour, at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, prior to coming into court, did you have an opportunity to review the stenographic record of the 14th Session of the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could have Prosecution Exhibit 709 on the monitor. And, specifically, I would like e-court pages 32 in English and 24 in B/C/S. I see there's a portion of the text in the English that goes over to the next page, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Starcevic, could you read to yourself the text that is in front of you. I'm just waiting, Mr. Starcevic, to enable the Trial Chamber the opportunity to read the full text that I will be referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is some of the text that carries over to the next page. I think that is a -- I am not confident -- could you scroll up in that, in the English version, please. Is this page 33 in the English text? Yes, okay. That's the correct text. Your Honours, I will be inquiring only on the text through the conclusion of that first paragraph under Momcilo Perisic, just for your information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Starcevic, in the text before you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just have to observe that, again, these two pages do not correspond, the B/C/S and the English version. They do not correspond to each other. If Mr. Harmon would like to ask questions that refer to the B/C/S page, I believe he should go a page back in English. But I don't know, of course, what his intentions are.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, I am told I have the right pages, so let me just confirm that. If we could go back to page 32 and scroll down. Yes, that is the correct page in English so ... and then we had the correct page in English on the -- Your Honours observed as well. So -- now if this -- since I can't read B/C/S, but since I do see in the first paragraph of the B/C/S the number 3612, I'm assuming I have the corresponding text. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Starcevic, I would invite your comments on this text that you have read, that's before you.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: This text obviously deals with resolving the problem of how to treat members of the army in the Republic of Serbian Krajina. However, that is not explicitly mentioned anywhere, but from the context we can infer that this relates to those men who are there. And it would appear that these are efforts to find some sort of solution so that those people can enjoy certain rights that otherwise they wouldn't have, if they did not retain their status in the army of the -- in the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Insofar as the text -- I want to read a portion of this text to you, Mr. Starcevic. It says under -- on this page that's before you, under Momcilo Perisic. It says: "We appoint them here. They not actually here but are performing their duties where they are stationed." And then if we scroll down a bit, Slobodan Milosevic says: "That's right, but only a single copy of this should stay with you." And Mr. Perisic says: "In our orders, for instance, we write to them. The commander of such-and-such unit shall be deployed in a training corps which is supposed to be here but in fact he is going over there." Can you comment on the text that I have just read to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From what the witness already said, I concluded that he was doing some guesswork. The witness can only infer something from what he has read but he doesn't have any direct knowledge. So his answer to the next question will again be speculation and guessing, and I don't think we will get a relevant answer, other than his opinion on what is stated there, which, of course, comes down to speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me rephrase the question, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, is there a law or set of laws that you're familiar with that would permit a VJ soldier to be assigned to a duty post in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia when, in fact, the actual deployment is to a different country?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: There is something similar to that. It's not exactly what you've said, but you could see it in that light. But only in the event that a military person is being sent for training abroad. That is the only situation where he would retain the status within the country and all the rights that come with it because that would be considered a temporary deployment abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me explore with you for a moment, Mr. Starcevic, transfers abroad. Under VJ law, under what circumstances can a VJ member be assigned to a post abroad?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Before Mr. Starcevic answers that question, we can go back in public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me repeat the question, Mr. Starcevic. Under VJ law, under what circumstances can a VJ member be assigned to a post abroad?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: This is only indirectly defined in the section on the pay of military persons in the Law on the Army of Yugoslavia, which defines exactly in which instances a professional soldier who is performing duties abroad, in what circumstances that individual can be remunerated. And as far as I can recall, there are three possible instances. The first one being when a professional soldier is assigned to a post abroad, to a diplomatic or consular mission of Yugoslavia abroad. The second case would be when a military person is assigned to a post abroad, in keeping with international treaties that Yugoslavia had concluded. And the third case would be where a military person is sent for training abroad. But in this last case, this person would only receive a sort of a stipend and that would be equal to his normal pay and perhaps somewhat larger during the period of his schooling abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we return to Prosecution Exhibit 197, the Law on the Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Starcevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what I'm interested in is -- on the screen -- I am interested in Articles -- Article 79 and 80.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, could you direct your attention to Article 79 and Article 80, and can you identify for the Court how these articles relate to my previous question?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: These two articles precisely define, as far as I understand them, what I have explained in my earlier answer. Article 79, in paragraph 2, relates to individuals who are assigned to a duty -- no, I apologise. This is paragraph 3. This relates to a person who is assigned to a diplomatic consular office abroad or required to perform tasks and duties resulting from international agreements, international agreements in which Yugoslavia is a party to. And Article 80 refers to an officer being sent abroad for schooling.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Are there any other legal provision that apply to transfers of VJ soldiers abroad, beside these two provisions you have cited to us?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Perisic -- Mr. Perisic. I apologise to Mr. Perisic and to Mr. Starcevic. Mr. Starcevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic is on his feet and is going to defend that statement. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Mr. Harmon's on page 40, line 8, I believe, again, that Mr. Harmon actually drew his own conclusions and asked the witness to just confirm them. The witness was talking about pay and not about transfer, and I think that this question is leading the witness to answer in a certain way. I can, of course, clarify this in my cross-examination but I think this entire article actually refers to pay and not to transfer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Lukic, originally Mr. Harmon asked about performing duties abroad. The witness said that performance is only indirectly referred to in the section that deals with pay, so that's why we are in the section that deals with pay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, let me now turn to a topic that you've alluded to a number of times and that relates --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you do that, I just want to have a real look at Article 79.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If we could go back to that page, please, Mr. Registrar [sic]. Sir, you have said that a soldier can be sent abroad and receive payment either for training - we see that in Article 80 - or when he is in consular duties, or when he is going on duties related to international treaties to which the country was a party. This first paragraph of Article 79 seems to have something additional. Wouldn't you agree with that? That an officer can be assigned on duty outside the army and be paid compensation, just assigned on duty.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I agree with you that there is an possibility for a soldier being assigned to a duty outside the army. However, the first two paragraphs of Article 79 do refer to assignment outside the army but not abroad. As far as assignments abroad are concerned, paragraph 3 is a form of lex specialis. The first two paragraphs refer to assignment of professional soldier to duties in various organs and organisations within the country. For instance, the service in the Ministry of Defence is considered service within the military. The same is true of service in some companies that are involved in the production of weapons and military equipment. That, too, can be such an instance. The same is true of service in some other institutions which are of interest for the defence or the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, I want to now turn to the topic of orders, because you have alluded on at least two occasions to orders and the results or consequences of orders. First of all, Mr. Starcevic, in the military sense, what is an order?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Again, this is a question that does not really differentiate between, "naredba," order, and "naredjenje," command or order again. In my understanding, in our military legal system, a "naredba" is a general regulation or a specific regulation that defines the responsibilities of and duties and rights of individuals. In other words, it should be viewed as a regulation that is adopted within administrative procedure, and this is provided for -- there is a specific procedure that has to be applied here. This has to be in compliance with the Law on the Administrative Procedure in Serbia and Yugoslavia, which also provides for complaints of individual who are dissatisfied with certain aspects and so on. So from that point of view, a "naredjenje," a command, means issuing operational command. So a "naredjenje" command is a provision or a document that is part of the chain of command. And there are special regulations in the rules of the service of the Army of Yugoslavia that provide for this, as well as at other statues involving commanding. This does not mean, of course, that in such instances there is no degree of protection provided for the persons who receive such orders, but, as a matter of principle such orders, "naredjenje," cannot be postponed. They have to be implemented, and the complaint can only be submitted after they have been implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. I want to stay very basic and very fundamental on this, Mr. Starcevic. Are orders, whether they are -- I think you use the term navidjenje [phoen] and "naredjenje" is that --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. So there's two types of orders. Is -- nevertheless, are both types of orders issued by superior officers?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: In some cases, some civilians serving, for example, in the Ministry of Defence are authorised to issue "naredba," orders, as administrative acts, for example, the minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Other than those exceptional circumstances, let me ask you then: Is a subordinate, then, who receives an order, be it "naredjenje" or "naredba," required to follow and obey the order?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now are there any -- are there any exceptions when a subordinate is not required to follow an order?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: There is an exception when the superior issuing the order expects perhaps the subordinate not to execute the order. Under the law, there are exceptions from the duty to carry out an order. Actually, there is an obligation to refuse to carry out an order. For example, if the execution of an order would lead to the commission of a criminal act, the subordinate is duty-bound to expressly refuse to carry out such an order and to take other measures. In some instances, when the order would represent a violation of the law but not also a criminal act at the same time, then the subordinate has the right to request that the order be issued in written form. When we're talking about orders such as general enactments, in the majority of cases appeal is permitted against the order, and in that case, the order is not carried out until the appeal is resolved, except in the case when it is provided under the law that the appeal proceeding would not postpone the actual execution of the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 43, line 24, the witness said in response Mr. Harmon's question that in principle, yes, in principle. This is what I heard the witness literally say. Perhaps that should be clarified. Perhaps that question should be put to the witness again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought I did hear that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We're referring, I take it, Mr. Lukic, to the part that says "Previous translation continues" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The "yes," at line 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- and it's not reported what the evidence is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No. The answer at line 24 which says, "Yes," the witness actually said, "In principle, yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I see. Well, I'm willing to accept what -- you know, for the record, what the Court heard and what is not reflected in this. I'm perfectly happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It just so happens that I did hear him say in principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's fine. I'm happy to accept that and the record can be corrected accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, so, Mr. Starcevic, you made a distinction between orders that are general enactments and orders that are command orders; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I want to direct -- I want to go back to Exhibit 197, if I can, and -- which is the Law on the Army. And I would like to direct your attention, Mr. Starcevic, to Article 154.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if we could have 154 in the English version. It is -- yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, can you, Mr. Starcevic, interpret Article 154? First of all, what kind -- what kind of documents does this apply to?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: This applies to orders as individual enactments deciding on the rights and duties of individual officers. Article 154 actually represents the procedure that is defined for the adoption of those enactments or the resolution of those enactments. For example, paragraph 1 states that the documents on promotion, transfer and assignment of professional officers and non-commissioned officers does not have to contain a statement of reasons. In paragraph 2, it is noted in which cases the appeal does not postpone or delay the execution of the enactments. And paragraph 3 refers to enactments, in relation to which legal protection cannot be invoked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So paragraph 2, Mr. Starcevic, relating to assignments and transfers, does it in fact allow for an appeal but only after the order has been executed?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid that it's not quite like that. It is not as precise as that. It does allow an appeal to be lodged and does not define a deadline for doing that, but the appeal itself does not postpone the execution of that particular order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we turn to Prosecution Exhibit 1896.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, let's, first of all, take some time to look at the first page. Apparently in B/C/S it's a two-page document, so if we could give you an opportunity to look at, first of all, the first page, and the Court as well, and then the second page. If you would just let me know when you want to go to the second page, Mr. Starcevic. You need to go to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page, then? Or go to the bottom of this first page. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can we go back? I wasn't clear whether we had the complete text in sight. Can we go back to the first page so Mr. Starcevic can confirm that he has read the whole text on the first page. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, then, if you want to read the second page of this document then -- okay. Have you --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've looked at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, if we go to first page we can see that this document is -- are minutes from an official talk about a transfer to the VRS, which talk occurred in the Drina Corps command. Now, just -- do you know what -- in what army the Drina Corps command is a formation?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You need to go to the -- that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you, are you ... I'm referring to the top paragraph, Mr. Starcevic. Is the Drina Corps a formation in -- in which army, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know, but based on this document, it can be concluded that this is a corps in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
