utterances.text: Okay. Now, in this instance, this document, what is Colonel Erak complaining about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of questions like this, we can get answers from this witness about what he reads in the document. What I see, Mr. Harmon is asking the witness questions about facts on which he has no direct knowledge, but the witness is supposed to be a fact witness, facts that he saw himself, heard, or has any kind of personal experience, so now the witness has embarked on assumptions because he doesn't have any direct knowledge about them. So basically the witness is being asked expert-type questions that he is not able to answer. The witness can be asked what -- who is doing what here, but he is not authorised to provide the Trial Chamber with assumptions about what happened after he left, and this document clearly is dated September 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I intend to do with this document -- first of all, I don't want to lead with my questioning. Second of all, I'm trying to identify the type of order that we have been discussing. I'm trying to get the witness to identify, if he can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The type of order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think that what you are saying now is a more legitimate question. But what had you asked, Mr. Harmon, was -- and unfortunately, the objection is completely irrelevant to what you were doing. You said: "Now in this instance, in this document, what is Colonel Erak complaining about?" Now, that I thought we can read that in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No problem. I can --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you characterize, Mr. Starcevic, the type of order that Colonel Erak is complaining about? You have identified two different types of orders for us in your examination. Are you able to determine what type of order he is complaining about? Is it "naredba" or "naredjenje"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a crucial question to which I put my previous crucial objection, and I assume that this is the way that Mr. Harmon plans to go through the documents he prepared with this witness. But I think this question is put to the witness and will make the witness speculate. The witness is a fact witness, not an expert and he is being asked to comment on something about which he does not have personal information or knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think -- of course, the witness doesn't have personal knowledge about Colonel Erak. However, he does -- has described two different types of orders. He has identified the provision in the law that relates to a specific element that I -- I don't want to lead the witness, but is related to -- earlier to a provision in the law about certain types of orders and appeals. That's all I'm trying to get out of this set of questions. So I think it's a fair question to ask him, if he is able to identify and characterize the type of order that we're talking about in this instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Objection overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, are you able to determine the type of order that Colonel Erak was objecting to?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I also have to say that this is not immediately evident from this document, but it can be concluded that he did receive an order on a transfer and that he is appealing this order. If we're asking what sort of an order it is, then my answer is if it is an order on the transfer, then it is a "naredba." It is the order that applies to the rights and duties of individuals. So it is an order pertaining to the sphere of administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Now, two provisions that are cited by -- a law that are either referred to directly or indirectly in this document are found in -- the first is found in subpart A, where Colonel Erak says, and I quote: "No one asked me for an opinion regarding my transfer to the 30th Personnel Centre. I have been transferred seven times so far." Mr. Starcevic, is there a basis in law or in the regulations that would support Mr. -- Colonel Erak's assertion relating to being transferred seven times?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Without his consent, do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Without his consent. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not sure about that under this law. This was the text in the previous law that regulated this, but in this particular law, there is no explicit reference to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which particular law are you talking about which you say there is no reference to, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This law, the Law on the Army, which went into effect in October 1993. Or, rather, May, 1994. The previous law did have an explicit provision on this, this one, that the second one does not. But I do recall that a regulation was being drafted on the application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Erak also refers to Article 58 with the Law on the Army. And he says: "I have been transferred to the Army of the RS in accordance with Article 58 of the Law on the Army of Yugoslavia, and on the same ground, I should not have and could not have been transferred to the 30th Personnel Centre." Now, can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I saw that comment, and I must admit that I was convinced that there was such a provision. Evidently I was thinking of the old law. Now I see, a little bit late, that this law, the new law, does not contain such a provision and that is why I don't understand why it is stated that he should not have executed it according to Article 158, unless this was regulated separately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... Article 58.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I was going next call up. Can we have Article --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, the text, first of all, says according to Article 158. My translation in subpart B of the English says Article 58, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we refer to -- could we take a look at Article 1 -- I'm sorry, Article 58 in Exhibit Prosecution 197.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you explain, Mr. Starcevic, explain Article 58.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: It seems to me that it is absolutely clear, and it says that a professional officer or a non-commissioned officer may be transferred in the course of his duty. The transfer would mean that he would need to change his place of residence. Only if the change of residence is implied in the sense of this law, it means that it is a transfer, and there are no limitations in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How long -- can a transfer under Article 58, does it have a limit the duration, how long it can last?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: A difference should be made between a transfer and a temporary assignment. A transfer is a lasting condition; you're moving from one position to another, from one place of residence to another. And perhaps you would never return to your previous post. But paragraph 3 talks about a temporary assignment. So, formally, are you not changing the place of residence. You are only temporarily being assigned to a position or duty that happens to be in a different location, not the location of your residence. Or perhaps not even your place of residence, but perhaps you're being reassigned to a different unit and that could still be in your place of residence. So when we're talking about this second case, temporary assignment, the place of residence is irrelevant. Temporary assignment can last for up to a year at the longest within a five-year period, meaning that somebody can, in a five-year period, be temporarily assigned to duties a number of times, but not longer than one year each time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. And finally in this document, if we go to subpart F --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could we go back to Prosecution Exhibit 1896, the minutes of the talk about the transfer to the 30th Personnel Centre. Could we take a look at subpart --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you going to be long on that point?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm happy to break here, Your Honours. I won't be long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Finish up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can we turn to subpart F, then, of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, just focus your attention on subpart F. And I just want you to expand, if you will, or explain to the Court what Mr. Erak says. He says he has fulfilled his statutory duty "because I have been at the front for nine months incessantly. In case my appeal is not granted, I will be forced to ask for my right at a court of law." Did Colonel Erak have a right to go a court of law on this kind of a order of transfer?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I have to say again that we're now drawing conclusions from an official conversation which is actually not the enactment that this pertains to. So this paragraph F as well as the contents of what Mr. Erak is stating are a little bit confusing, so it is not quite clear whether we're talking about a transfer or a temporary assignment here. Because paragraph F suggests that this is a temporary assignment. This expression "to return" is difficult to interpret in any other way, other than that he was temporarily assigned to a place, but he also then refers to transfer. So the whole thing is a little bit confusing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Very briefly, if we can just stay with the temporary assignment, would he have recourse to a court of law on an appeal on an order of temporary assignment?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: In the specific case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the question could have been put in a more general way but from what the witness said previously, he cannot be asked to make any conclusions on the basis of this document. So he could be asked a general question of whether there is a right to appeal in such a case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's precisely what I thought I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure, Mr. Lukic, that what you -- I can't see the difference between what you are suggesting and what the question was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was listening to the B/C/S translation but I understood that the question referred to based on this document whether he was entitled to submit a complaint. But I think that kind of question can only be put based on the law, whether a complaint can be submitted. In my view, such a question can be asked because the witness himself said that did he not have any direct knowledge about this particular document. This would be calling for speculation, in my view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You understand what he is saying. Not based on the document but based on the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Based on the law, correct. I will rephrase the question, then, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would an individual who has been temporarily assigned to a duty post have, in an appeal, a right to apply for his rights in a court of law?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, now we are in the area of interpreting laws. I think not, because it does not have to do on deciding on somebody's rights or duties, but, rather, about their status in service, as it is at the moment. However, he is entitled to submitting a complaint if the temporary assignment is longer than provided for in the law, and in this particular case that would also depend on the order on the basis of which he is reassigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no further questions on this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would that be a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Will Your Honours go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have Prosecution Exhibit 1895 placed on the screen. Initially, if we could have page 1 of both the English and the B/C/S placed on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, this is a document that is identified in the upper left-hand corner of the English version as an order, number 5-76/1. Have you seen this document before coming into court to testify?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would -- first of all, can you tell us what kind of an order. You have characterized two different types of orders, what kind of an order is this order?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Here we see again an order that is a general administrative enactment, appointing a professional officer to duty in a certain unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I want to go through this document so we can understand this documents and all the parties can. First of all, Mr. Starcevic, I refer you to the part -- subpart A that says: "Appointed as per the peacetime establishment." And what I'm going to do in this document, Mr. Starcevic, is take you through -- there are four categories identified in this document and I'm going to ask to you define what each of these categories means. So if we could start, please, with "appointed as per peacetime establishment." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: That means that pursuant to an order, Mr. Sekulic is appointed to -- to the duty of chief of training in the -- training and operations in the Belgrade garrison. But in fact what it says there is that is he appointed to a post in the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army, the 40th Personnel Centre unit, at the command of the Main Staff of that centre, as the chief of the department or section for operations and training in the Belgrade garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And -- but what is the terminology "appointed as per the peacetime establishment," what does that mean as opposed to what I will be showing in a few minutes, transfers, et cetera? Are you able to tell the Court precisely what an appointment as to the peacetime establishment means?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: That means in fact that this appointment, this position, is there according to the establishment, for that unit, in peacetime. Because sometimes establishment posts can differ in peacetime and in wartime, within units. There are also other instances that can be compared to wartime conditions. So in this particular instance, he is appointed to this post per peacetime establishment, the establishment that is in effect during peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. And where was he previously serving his duty, prior to this particular appointment?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: From this document, it would appear that even before this appointment he was on duty, or he was part of the 40th Personnel Centre, but we cannot see from this document on which position or what post he was appointed at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can we see from this document how he arrived at the position in the 40th Personnel Centre prior to this particular appointment? I refer you to the -- I refer you to the last paragraph, Mr. Starcevic.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But we cannot see how he actually came to be appointed to this position because that is not stated there. But we can see that he was transferred to the 40th Personnel Centre on order by the Chief of Staff of the Yugoslav Army; in other words, the same person who issued this order as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Now I want to go to page 76 in the English and page 66 in the B/C/S. We'll see another type of description. Can you see under the letter B it says: "Assigned and appointed as per peacetime establishment." What is the difference between this reference, "assigned and appointed," as opposed to the previous reference, which is just "appointed"?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: The difference is in that the gentleman that we are discussing here, Mr. Mihajlovic, in other words, was not posted at the 40th Personnel Centre before this order. He was in the 1st Administration, in the development and procurement department of the infantry department of the land forces. In other words, this same document re-assigns him from the previous unit to the 40th Personnel Centre, and at the same time, he is appointed to a certain post in that Personnel Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So, in this case, Mr. Simo Mihajlovic is appointed to the 40th Personnel Centre, Main Staff, as an administrative officer in the supply section; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I have difficulty reading so I need some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now if we can look at another type of an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could go to -- if we could turn to page 78 in the English and page 68 in the B/C/S. Your Honours may recall this is a rather large document and it pertains to 141 persons, and so --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can we take a look at this, then, section, Mr. Starcevic, and I am looking at the letter -- it should be C. It says: "Transferred." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What does that mean in the context of this order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Wait a minute. I'm not seeing C on this page in English. I see G, "Transfer."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's a typographical -- I mean, that's an error. I said it should be C. It is G, and so I apologise for the translation. It should be C. But --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters comment: It is G in B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We both stand corrected, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, the letter G, then. Thank you to the interpreters for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, now we see a reference to certain people being transferred in this order. And if you could help us with what some of the meaning of that is. Can I just -- before you give me your answer, because it is very helpful for to us look at the illustrations that follow. On the English all we have is the "transferred" but --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we get the text, then, on the next page as well to this person who has been transferred. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Starcevic, what does "transferred" mean, and where is Mr. Pero Vucetic transferred to and from?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: A transfer means that Mr. Vucetic, up until this order, served in the garrison in Podgorica, in this particular instance, and then pursuant to this order, he was transferred to the Belgrade garrison to a certain unit, a unit of the 40th Personnel Centre, but his post and duty per establishment was not determined. Rather, it was left to the officer in charge, the officer in charge of that centre. And that is in keeping with the order that we discussed earlier, that the chief of the General Staff or other officers to whom he delegates those duty, they perform certain duties. In this particular instance, because this is a non-commissioned officer, the officer to whom this duty was delegated was of a lower rank than in some other instances. And because he is transferred, there is also a request for the change of his residence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now the reason that is given in the transfer of Mr. Vucetic is, and I quote: "He is transferred according to service requirements effective 6 January 1994, when he reported for duty." Can you assist us in the meaning of being "transferred according to service requirements"? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I cannot explain for service requirements can be different. It can be vacated position that he would need to fill, a new position. The reasons could be different. But I would like to just remind you that, pursuant to the Law on the Army, transfer enactments in principle are not explained. Service requirements imply the interests of the army service to allocate persons to different posts or positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. And I --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would like to note, Your Honours, for the record, there appears to an omission in case of Mr. Vucetic on the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Starcevic, you can assist us. In the B/C/S version it indicates that this gentleman, Mr. Vucetic, was transferred to the Belgrade garrison. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That language is missing, Your Honour, I note, in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you look at the top of the English version as it stands now, the very first line says to Belgrade garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I see. Well, then -- okay. Okay. Well, then I'm corrected, then, Your Honour. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now if we could turn finally to page 83 of the English and page 72 of the B/C/S. We see under subpart D, the words "temporarily assigned." Can you assist us in the meaning of what "temporary assignment" is?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: That implies that a professional soldier would be sent to certain assignments for a pre-determined period of time, in a unit that was not a part of his own home unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So in this case, the individual Mr. Krnjeta Milos, was temporarily assigned to the Yugoslav Army General Staff, 40th Personnel Centre, Main Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the basis, the legal basis for that assignment, can you identify what the legal basis is for that assignment, Mr. Starcevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Article 58 of the Law on the Army of Yugoslavia, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, does Article 58, paragraph 3, of the Law on the Army, Yugoslav Army, authorise the transfer of an individual from one unit to the army of a different country or service in a different country?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that, again, we're in a situation where the witness is interpreting an article. That is actually your job. The witness is going asked to interpret Article 58 in his way but actually that is the job of the Trial Chamber, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the witness is -- can speak directly to Article 58. He participated in the drafting of this legislation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My problem with this kind of question is that we are lawyers in the courtroom and we read and interpret the laws, so we're asking the witness to interpret this. But, actually, this is a matter for the Trial Chamber, the matter of interpreting matters like this, and what weight to attach to that. I understand when we're talking about ballistics experts or other fields when the Trial Chamber might need assistance, but I think in this matter, I think there is no need for that, and that the answer that the witness could give would not really have that much weight or importance when the Chamber is actually weighing this evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Objection upheld.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, if we could go back into -- I'm sorry. If we could go into public session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have Prosecution Exhibit 1527 on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, is this a -- can you tell the Court what the nature of this document is?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Again, this is an order which is, in essence, an administrative enactment, temporarily assigning Mr. Sladojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: To -- assigning him to where?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: To the 30th Personnel Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, could we take a look at Prosecution Exhibit 1524, have that on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Sladojevic [sic], this is an order with -- signed by General Perisic and it has a terminology, "redeployed and assigned as per peacetime establishment." Can you tell us what that means, that language?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: This, again, as in the previous cases we analysed, it means that Mr. Sladojevic is leaving the garrison or the place where he was on duty up until then, to a different garrison, or to a different location, so he is changing his place of residence, and by this act, at the same time, he is being assigned to a specific duty in the new unit, in this new post and place of residence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Sladojevic [sic], where had -- I'm sorry, Mr. Starcevic. Where had Mr. Sladojevic been assigned prior to his redeployment?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Before the transfer, Mr. Sladojevic was working at the 40th Personnel Centre, at the Belgrade garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And let me refer you to the language below, at the bottom of the English, and I'd like you to assist me in understanding what this means. It says: "As per peacetime establishment to date: Commander 11th Corps of the Yugoslav Army General Staff, 40th Personnel Centre, FC of Colonel, P G5 as of 10 November 1993, Belgrade garrison." So can you assist us with that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Sladojevic was the commander of the 11th Corps, which is part of the 40th Personnel Centre of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. By establishment of that corps, the duty to which he was appointed, the rank of colonel was required and the position -- or the post group was established. So all of this refers to the corps or the training centre in the Belgrade garrison. His place of -- or duty post was in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I have two questions, Mr. Sladojevic [sic]. To your knowledge, was there an 11th Corps posted -- 11th Corps of the Yugoslav Army posted in Belgrade at any time during your experience as a military officer?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell, because, as far as I can remember, while I was serving in the army, the organisation of the Yugoslav Army was different. The army was organised in to the -- the structure of the army was organised into armies, various armies, and then subordinated units, but I really cannot speak to this. The reorganisation, I think, followed after I left the army. But as far as can I recall, some corps were in Belgrade, but this one, I believe would, have come after I left my post in the army, but in any case, I wouldn't know the number or the particular corps that was in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, is there any legal authority, Mr. Starcevic, that would permit General Perisic the authority to transfer a soldier, a VJ soldier, from an army in the -- in the RSK, in the Republika Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm talking theoretically, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no. Mr. Lukic is on his feet. That's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood this question to be theoretical but I would still have the same complaint that I had earlier. We have the law -- you have the law in front of you, the law has been adopted into evidence and you are the ones who are going to assess and give it certain weight. And now, my colleague is asking the witness to actually interpret those laws, and I believe that that is outside of the framework of your instructions yesterday, your decision yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will rephrase the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, are there any provisions in the law that you're aware of that would permit General Perisic or any other officer to give an order of redeployment to a person serving in a different army? Are there any provisions of the law that would authorise that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it seems to me that this question has not been reformulated, and I believe that Mr. Harmon has repeated the same form of question. He is just calling the witness to interpret the law, and I believe that that is your exclusive right as the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not asking the Court to interpret the law. I'm asking this witness who knows the law and helped draft the law to identify what provisions, if any, apply to the circumstances I have put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, I don't see any request for identification in your question, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, my question was, are there any provisions in the law which I'm asking him to identify those provisions in the law; at least that's what I intended by that question. I can rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you identify any provisions in the law, Mr. Starcevic, that would permit an officer serving in the VJ to give a redeployment order to an officer serving in a different army in a different country?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. I was saying to Mr. Lukic that I was looking at him but I'm still reading what the question was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My essential objection, Your Honour, is that you, as the Trial Chamber, are the one who is to assess and give weight to a law and here the witness is being asked to assist you that sense, and to interpret the law. I understand Mr. Harmon's argument that Mr. Starcevic is one of the individuals who actually drafted these laws, but with his answers, where he would interpret the laws, he cannot be, in my view, of any assistance to the Trial Chamber, and according to me, that goes to the very merit of this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the question as couched now lately, the very last couching is somewhat different. First of all, the witness is not being asked to interpret the law. He is being asked to identify a provision in the law. So he must refer us to law so-and-so, article so-and-so, paragraph so-and-so. The Chamber will read that law and decide whether he is right in saying that is the law that allows a redeployment. And, secondly, the question relates to redeployment of an officer serving in a different army in a different country. We haven't been shown that before, and this is -- that last part is -- is different from the questions that Mr. Harmon had asked earlier. As couched like that, the question will stand, and the answer that I expect is -- that we be referred to a specific law.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you -- you can answer the question, Mr. Starcevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I had asked you, Mr. Starcevic, can you identify any provision in the law that would authorise a VJ officer to give an order to redeploy an officer from a different country serving in a different army.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: In my understanding, there is no such provision.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we have looked at a series of three orders dealing with appointments, transfers, appointment and transfer, et cetera. And those orders, in summary, in large measure dealt with appointments and transfers to the 30th or the 40th Personnel Centre. Were members of the VJ who were assigned or appointed or transferred to the 30th and 40th Personnel Centres members of the VJ, according to the law?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Starcevic, I want to change the topic a bit, and I wanted to ask you about volunteering while a member of the Yugoslav Army. Under law, are there provisions in the law that permit a VJ soldier to volunteer for service to a particular post?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: In principle, yes. A soldier may volunteer for service to a particular post. I think that it can be interpreted that a soldier may volunteer or ask to be appointed to a certain duty, but we have to draw a difference between an appointment, in which case he would have to be appointed according -- following a certain procedure, which also implies that there would be an enactment or a document from a superior officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you refer to us that law, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the Law on the Army, and this issue is somewhat broader than it is defined in this law, which deals with the issue of volunteers, and I will now try to find that particular provision.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, maybe --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that would be Article 15 of the Law on the Army, but it relates, indeed, to volunteers within the service and not those who volunteer to carry out a certain task who are already professional soldiers or who are already serving in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, can we have Article 15 in this Prosecution Exhibit 197. Can we have Article 15 on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, you referred to soldiers within the army being able to volunteer. Is that covered by Article 15?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, can you explain to the Court Article 15 and what it means.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Article 15 regulates the manner or manners in which the Army of Yugoslavia may be reinforced, or manned. There are three paragraphs in this article which relate to reinforcement by volunteers and those are the second, third, and fourth paragraphs. In the first place, the reinforcements with volunteers is, under the law, possible during a state of war, imminent threat of war, or during a state of emergency. Further on -- furthermore, volunteers may be only those individuals who are not subject to military service, to compulsory military service, or individuals who are subject to compulsory military service but who have not been issued a wartime establishment post in the event of war. In any case, all such volunteers would be part of the army, and from that moment on, they would, in every respect, have the same rights and responsibilities as all other military persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Just staying focussed on Article 15, it, in the second paragraph, puts certain conditions before the army can be reinforced with volunteers. Now, a state of war, imminent threat of war, and a state of emergency. Is that -- are those conditions defined in the law?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the law, and I think even in the constitution it is defined when such states may be proclaimed, and I think in all these event -- in some of these events, the authorised person who can proclaim such a state would be the president of the republic, whereas in some other instances it would be the parliament. I'm not absolutely certain because I don't have the constitution in front of me --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: -- but the primary responsibility or authority --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't mean to cut you off. But just to assist you, if I could direct your attention to Article 4 in the Law on Defence, which is Prosecution Exhibit 1183.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If that could be displayed on the monitor so we can just clarify the legal parameters of Article 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Does Article 4, Mr. Starcevic, cover the language -- identify the language that is found in Article 15?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is the article I meant, and it actually defines that the Federal Assembly is the one that will proclaim one of these states as the condition where the army can be reinforced by volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, to your knowledge, Mr. Starcevic, between the years 1992 and 1995, was a state of war or imminent threat of war or a state of emergency declared in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I think it wasn't. But I'm not absolutely certain. You know, I am an elderly man.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, now I want to change the issue of volunteers slightly, okay? Because Article 15 from its text appears to deal with volunteers reinforcing the VJ. I want to change the issue slightly. Okay. I'm talking about an active duty officer serving in the VJ. Are there provisions of the law that cover an active duty officer in the VJ volunteering to serve, either inside another unit in the VJ or outside of the country? Are there legal provisions that you can direct us to that cover that set of circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: It is my view that legal language has to be precise, and in that sense, there is no provision regulating a situation where an individual may be a volunteer in that kind of situation, which does not mean, of course, that professional active-duty officers do not have the right to initiate their promotion to -- or a transfer to another unit. The assignment to a different duty is a whole different story. Now, whether such an initiative will be accepted, that is a different issue. But they are not, strictly speaking, and in the language of the law, volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In that -- if a professional military soldier's initiative is accepted, what kind of an instrument regulates service under those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: One of those orders that we discussed earlier. Depending on where they are going, they're either transferred or transferred and appointed, or assigned or appointed to another duty, so it would depend on -- it would be on a case-to-case basis but it would have to be pursuant to one such administrative enactment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Is there any provision of the law that permits an active-duty officer serving in the army to go to a different country and serve in a -- in a different army or in a different country that you can point out?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I will say it again, as I already have. In my view, there is no such provision.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Then let me -- thank you very much, Mr. Starcevic. I have some additional questions in respect of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: First of all, I'd like to get -- have Prosecution Exhibit 847 on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, just acquaint yourself, if you would, for a moment, with this particular document. Are you familiar with this document; have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I think I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 29th of January, 2001, issued by the supreme military court and it is in response or it relates to a complaint filed by Colonel Zarko Ljubojevic in a matter relating to his claim for compensation for unused annual leave. Did you review this yesterday, Mr. Starcevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, could we turn to page 2 of the English and page 2 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you initially, Mr. Starcevic, what was it that Mr. Ljubojevic was seeking in this legal action?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is it obvious that Ljubojevic had been prevented from using his annual leave several years in a row, and he notes that he was prevented from using his annual leave because he took part in some combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can I direct your attention and may I direct the Court's attention -- let me direct your attention first to the bottom paragraph in B/C/S, and the Court's attention to the language that starts in the second paragraph, starting with: "In this specific case ..." Mr. Starcevic, can I ask you to comment on these -- on this judgement, this part of the judgement that I have referred you to?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, obviously the Court in its statement of reasons states its reasons why it overturned the decision of the lower court where he was denied compensation for unused annual leave. And in the statement of reasons of this judge, he -- he was established that Ljubojevic was assigned to serve outside the Army of Yugoslavia and that this is a case where provisions of the law that are in effect for people serving in the Army of Yugoslavia and that are applicable to such active-duty persons should be applicable to him, too, and that, as such, he would be entitled to such compensation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, insofar as this judgement is concerned, Mr. Starcevic, did the court establish as a matter of this judgement, whether Mr. Ljubojevic, who was serving elsewhere, was a member of the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that this question was couched in such a way that the witness actually read the statement of reasons, and now, again, he is asked -- the witness is asked to comment on what is written. So, in this manner, we know that the witness has read that this man was outside the service and now he is asked whether he was considered to be in service, and I think with such questions and such answers, we gain nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll withdraw the question, Your Honour. Could we turn to another judgement. That is Prosecution Exhibit 822.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to see this document, Mr. Starcevic, prior to coming in to testify? This is a judgement of the Second Municipal Court in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what was this lawsuit about?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: In this case, Mr. Milosevic submitted a request to have his right to compensation recognised, due to physical pains and reduced work capability that he suffered, and general living condition, and he is asking for a specific amount of damages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we turn to page 8 in the English and page 7 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can I, Mr. Starcevic, direct you to language --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can't see the top of the page, I'm afraid, on the B/C/S, so I -- we're on the wrong page. Page 7 is what I thought I had asked for in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: While we're getting page 7, Your Honour, can I direct Your Honours' attention to the middle paragraph: "The court considered the objection ..." And, Mr. Starcevic, I think that is the language that is found at the top of page 7. Starts with: "The court considered the objection that the accused ..." et cetera. Could you read that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can I invite your comments, Mr. Starcevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: It seems clear to me that the court rejected the objection of a lack of passive legitimacy and took the position that the gentleman was not a member of the Army of Republika Srpska but a member of the Army of Yugoslavia, who was sent to the combat zone in the environs of Sarajevo, and, for that reason, he did have the right to submit this complaint.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. I'd like to show you another document but I need to go into private session for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session. 6 [Private session] [Confidentiality lifted by order of the Chamber]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have Exhibit 1902 on the monitor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Have you seen this document before, Mr. Starcevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And can you -- this is a decree dated the 16th of June, 1994, exceptionally promoting to the rank of colonel general Ratko Mladic, who is -- it says the 30th Personnel Centre Main Staff commander. Can you, first of all, tell us what the effect of this decree would be in the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Simply from that point on, Ratko Mladic is an officer with the rank of colonel general in the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, the legal basis that is identified for this exceptional promotion is Article 136 of the constitution, and Article 46, paragraph 1, of the Law on the Armed Forces of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could return to the Law on the Army, Prosecution Exhibit 197, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would like to direct your attention, Mr. Starcevic, to Article 46.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I see this presents one of those difficult situations where only part of the article appears on the English at the bottom, so I -- when the Court is finished reading that element that appears in the bottom, if we could turn to the next page. Could we turn to the next -- second page then. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, can you explain to the Court Article 46 of the Law on the Army?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: The concept of exceptional promotion, under the law, is provided as a special institute, due to the exceptional contribution of some officers. Article 46 actually regulates the authorities of different organs for exceptional promotion, depending on the rank. In this case, undoubtedly, the president of the republic would be the authorised body for such a promotion, because a person who has the rank of lieutenant-colonel general is being promoted to the rank of colonel general.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What -- what happens before a person is promoted to the rank of colonel general, in terms of this law? What does it say?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: In order to analyse that we would need a special rule adopted by the federal government pursuant to paragraph 3 of this article which deals with the procedure and the terms. Of course, what else is happening here, if that's what you meant, is that for this kind of promotion there should be a proposal by the chief of the General Staff for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm finished with this document. The next exhibit, if we could take a look at it, is Prosecution Exhibit 197 -- I'm sorry, 1905.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Starcevic, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And this is a document that's dated the 16th of June, 2001, and it is entitled -- has a caption, "Removed from the records of professional soldiers of the Yugoslav Army," and it identifies 26 individuals by name. Can you -- first of all, what is the meaning of "removed from the records of the professional soldiers of the Yugoslav Army"? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: It means that from that point on, in a formal legal sense they ceased to be professional soldiers in the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I see. Okay. And -- okay. Now, it also indicates under that language, "removed from the records of the professional soldiers of the Yugoslav Army," it says that these 26 individuals are filling posts in the Yugoslav Army General Staff 30th Personnel Centre. Do you have any comment, Mr. Starcevic, on that language?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: It simply means that they were removed from the records, and they cease to be officers of the Army of Yugoslavia and are serving in the -- in posts in the 30th Personnel Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the 30th Personnel Centre was a component part of the Yugoslav Army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We've already noted that earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what does that mean in respect of whether or not the 26 individuals identified in this document were in fact members of the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG STARCEVIC
utterances.text: From a formal legal aspect, they were in fact members of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no further questions at this point, Your Honour. I have questions tomorrow but I'm about to change topics. This would be a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then we will take a break. And before we do so let me just say to you, sir, that we are not done with you yet. Please come back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm told we are still in private session. May the Chamber please move into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. You probably do know this, sir, but it is just my duty to remind that you that you are under oath. You have not finished testifying. You may not talk to anybody about the case until you have finished your testimony. We'll come back tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning in the same court. So we will adjourn for now for the day. Court adjourned.
